meta.title: Computer Networks: Packets, Names & Trust
meta.interests: Agriculture, music, space, practical engineering and evidence-based technology

plan.title: Computer Networks: Packets, Names & Trust
plan.hook: A device can have Wi-Fi bars while a service still fails. Separate name lookup, transport, secure channels and application outcomes to diagnose the actual boundary.
objectives: Distinguish local links, IP routing, transport and application roles
Explain DNS caching, TCP delivery and uncertain request outcomes
Calculate simple transmission time while separating other delays
Write a layered service-diagnosis memo with evidence and bounded retries
prerequisites: Basic bits, bytes and time units; no network administration required

sections.heading: Separate a local connection from a working service
Names and addresses are different evidence
points: Limit: returned address is not service health

sections.heading: Delivery guarantees stop at a boundary
points: Application: defines messages and commit meaning
Retry: uncertain outcomes need idempotency or status

sections.heading: Bandwidth is not the same as latency
points: Serialization: packet bits divided by link rate

points: TLS: channel confidentiality, integrity and identity checks

sections.heading: Capstone: diagnose the failing boundary
points: Timeout: committed outcome may be uncertain
Memo: evidence, bounded retry and safe identifiers

sections.heading: Separate a local connection from a working service
sections.body:
A network request crosses several functions. A local link moves frames to a nearby device, such as an access point or router. Internet Protocol, or IP, provides packet addressing and forwarding across networks. A transport protocol connects application endpoints. The application defines what the request and response mean.

These functions can succeed or fail separately. Strong Wi-Fi signal indicates a local radio condition, not proof that DNS resolves a service, a remote route exists or an account can access the application. Likewise, a server responding with an application error is different from receiving no response at all.

Packets are units forwarded by the network; they are not necessarily complete user actions. A large response may span many packets. A router chooses a next hop based on forwarding information, rather than needing to understand the business meaning of the request.

**Try it:** Draw a device, local router and remote service. Annotate a failure in each function without claiming that a single signal-strength icon tests them all. This course uses a simplified layered model rather than one mandatory stack for every application.
sections.visual: The four panels describe functions with distinct evidence. The simplified layout does not imply every application uses the same transport.

questions.q: Why do strong Wi-Fi bars not prove a remote service works?
questions.hint: The icon observes one part of the path.
questions.answer: They concern the local radio link, while naming, routing, transport, server state and authorization are separate dependencies.

questions.q: Does one packet necessarily equal one complete user action?
questions.hint: Messages and packets have different boundaries.
questions.answer: No. An application action can span multiple messages and packets, and a packet does not by itself prove the action committed.

sections.heading: Names and addresses are different evidence
sections.body:
The Domain Name System, or DNS, maps names to records through a distributed hierarchy. A client commonly asks a recursive resolver, which may answer from cache or query other servers. Records can include addresses and other information; a name is not itself a permanent IP address.

Caching reduces repeated work. A time to live, or TTL, specifies how long a record can be reused under the protocol’s cache rules. A cached answer may outlast a server move until its allowed lifetime expires. Changing an authoritative record does not instantly replace every cached observation everywhere.

A successful lookup proves that a record was returned, not that the application at that address is available or authorized for the user. Conversely, accessing a bare IP instead of a name may fail virtual-host routing or certificate identity checks, so it is not always an equivalent application test.

**Try it:** In a fictional incident record, separate the requested name, returned record, resolver, timestamp and subsequent service result. Do not infer a global DNS outage from one client’s lookup without further evidence.
sections.visual: The resolver may answer from cache rather than contacting authority every time. A returned record remains a naming result, not an application acceptance result.

questions.q: Why can an old address remain visible after an authoritative change?
questions.hint: Other systems may retain valid cache entries.
questions.answer: Resolvers and clients can reuse cached records until their cache lifetime expires under the applicable rules.

questions.q: Why is testing a bare IP not always equivalent to the service name?
questions.hint: Names can be part of application routing and identity.
questions.answer: Virtual hosting and certificate verification can depend on the intended name, so an IP-only request may test a different path.

sections.heading: Delivery guarantees stop at a boundary
sections.body:
TCP supplies a reliable, ordered byte stream between endpoints while the connection remains viable. It detects loss and retransmits as needed. It does not preserve application message boundaries automatically, and successful byte delivery does not prove the receiving application committed a requested action.

UDP carries datagrams without TCP’s built-in ordered reliable-stream service. Applications can add their own reliability and congestion mechanisms on top. Modern protocols such as QUIC demonstrate why “uses UDP” does not imply that the complete application protocol has no reliability features.

A timeout can leave an operation’s outcome uncertain. The request may never have arrived, may still be processing, or may have committed while the response was lost. Blindly retrying a state-changing request can duplicate an action unless the application provides idempotency or a reliable status query.

**Try it:** Sketch a fictional appointment request with a request identifier. Design a retry rule that asks for the existing result before creating another appointment. Distinguish a transport reconnection from a guarantee of exactly-once business processing.
sections.visual: Transport delivery and application commit evidence are deliberately separate. A completed network exchange is not a universal transaction guarantee.
sections.diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 400"><rect x="1" y="1" width="798" height="398" rx="6" fill="#101a2a" stroke="#101a2a"/><text x="30" y="40" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="24" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Reliable delivery and application success differ</text><text x="30" y="70" fill="#a8b9d0" font-size="15" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">TCP provides an ordered byte stream, not an automatic transaction receipt.</text><rect x="55" y="125" width="325" height="195" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#a8b9d0"/><text x="71" y="155" fill="#69d9d0" font-size="19" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Transport evidence</text><text x="71" y="187" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="16" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Connection established</text><text x="71" y="214" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="16" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Bytes delivered in order</text><text x="71" y="241" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="16" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Retransmission may add delay</text><rect x="420" y="125" width="325" height="195" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#a8b9d0"/><text x="436" y="155" fill="#f8bf70" font-size="19" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Application evidence</text><text x="436" y="187" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="16" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Request validated</text><text x="436" y="214" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="16" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Action committed</text><text x="436" y="241" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="16" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Result recorded or queried</text><text x="30" y="377" fill="#a8b9d0" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">A timeout after sending a request can leave its application outcome uncertain.</text></svg>

questions.q: Does TCP byte delivery prove an application committed an action?
questions.answer: No. The application must validate, commit and report its own outcome; transport delivery alone does not establish that state.

questions.q: Why can retrying after timeout duplicate a booking?
questions.hint: The original may have committed before the response disappeared.
questions.answer: Without an idempotency key or status mechanism, a new request can create another action even when the original succeeded.

sections.heading: Bandwidth is not the same as latency
sections.body:
Bandwidth is a capacity rate, usually in bits per second. Latency is elapsed delay. Serialization time is how long it takes to put a packet’s bits onto a link; propagation is how long the signal travels. Queuing, processing and protocol exchanges add further delay.

A 1,500-byte packet has 12,000 bits before any additional link overhead. On a stated 10 Mbit/s link, serialization is 12,000 / 10,000,000 = 0.0012 s, or 1.2 ms. A 20 ms propagation path does not disappear if serialization becomes faster.

Throughput is the useful rate actually achieved. Shared capacity, losses, congestion control, server work and many small round trips can limit it below the nominal link rate. A bandwidth test alone may miss a slow name lookup or delayed application response.

**Try it:** Divide a hypothetical page load into name lookup, connection setup, server work and data transfer. Identify which parts might benefit from a faster last-mile link and which need different evidence. Keep one-way and round-trip times distinct; they are not interchangeable measurements.
sections.visual: The small serialization component and larger fictional propagation component share a time unit. A faster bit rate affects only some parts of total delay.
sections.diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 400"><rect x="1" y="1" width="798" height="398" rx="6" fill="#101a2a" stroke="#101a2a"/><text x="30" y="40" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="24" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Serialization and propagation are different delays</text><text x="30" y="70" fill="#a8b9d0" font-size="15" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">One 1,500-byte packet on a stated 10 Mbit/s link; no overhead or queues.</text><text x="195" y="167" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="17" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">Serialize packet</text><rect x="210" y="145" width="475" height="30" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#33445e"/><rect x="210" y="145" width="22.8" height="30" rx="6" fill="#69d9d0" stroke="#69d9d0"/><text x="697" y="167" fill="#69d9d0" font-size="17" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">1.2 ms</text><text x="195" y="257" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="17" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">Propagation example</text><rect x="210" y="235" width="475" height="30" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#33445e"/><rect x="210" y="235" width="380.0" height="30" rx="6" fill="#f8bf70" stroke="#f8bf70"/><text x="697" y="257" fill="#f8bf70" font-size="17" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">20 ms</text><text x="30" y="377" fill="#a8b9d0" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">12,000 bits / 10,000,000 bit/s = 1.2 ms. A faster link does not erase propagation.</text></svg>

questions.q: What is serialization time for the stated packet and link?
questions.answer: 1,500 × 8 / 10,000,000 s = 1.2 ms, excluding additional overhead and other delays.

questions.q: Why can a high-bandwidth connection still feel slow?
questions.answer: Propagation, queuing, protocol round trips, name lookup and server processing can dominate the user-visible delay.

sections.heading: A secure channel does not authorize every action
sections.body:
Transport Layer Security, or TLS, protects a connection against eavesdropping and tampering under its protocol assumptions. In a typical authenticated web connection, the client also verifies the server’s certificate identity for the intended name. Encryption without proper endpoint verification does not establish the same identity claim.

Authentication asks who or what is presenting credentials. Authorization asks what that identity may do. A correctly protected connection can carry a request that the application rejects for missing credentials, expired context or insufficient permission. A secure channel also cannot guarantee that an endpoint is honest or uncompromised.

Diagnostic records should preserve endpoint, time, response code and a safe request identifier. Avoid copying secrets into logs. A server response indicating authentication failure is evidence about the application boundary; repeatedly changing DNS or disabling certificate checks does not address that evidence.

**Try it:** Classify three fictional events: certificate identity mismatch; valid channel with missing login; valid login lacking edit permission. Write a separate next check for each. Keep transport trust and application permission visible as distinct questions.
sections.visual: TLS protects a defined communication channel. The application still has to validate identity context and permissions for the requested action.
sections.diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 800 400"><rect x="1" y="1" width="798" height="398" rx="6" fill="#101a2a" stroke="#101a2a"/><text x="30" y="40" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="24" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Transport protection has a defined boundary</text><text x="30" y="70" fill="#a8b9d0" font-size="15" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Conceptual TLS connection with authenticated server identity.</text><rect x="65" y="140" width="210" height="140" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#a8b9d0"/><text x="81" y="170" fill="#69d9d0" font-size="19" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Client</text><text x="81" y="202" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="16" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Checks identity</text><text x="81" y="229" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="16" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Protects records</text><rect x="310" y="175" width="180" height="65" rx="6" fill="#344459" stroke="#baa6ff"/><text x="400" y="215" fill="#baa6ff" font-size="19" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">TLS channel</text><rect x="525" y="140" width="210" height="140" rx="6" fill="none" stroke="#a8b9d0"/><text x="541" y="170" fill="#f8bf70" font-size="19" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Server</text><text x="541" y="202" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="16" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Receives request</text><text x="541" y="229" fill="#e5edf9" font-size="16" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Still validates access</text><text x="30" y="377" fill="#a8b9d0" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">Encryption does not prove the endpoint is honest or that the user is authorized for every action.</text></svg>

questions.q: Can a valid TLS connection still produce an access rejection?
questions.answer: Yes. The channel can work while the application rejects missing authentication or insufficient authorization.

questions.q: Why retain a safe request identifier instead of a credential in diagnostics?
questions.hint: You need correlation without exposing secrets.
questions.answer: A request identifier can correlate evidence across components while keeping passwords or tokens out of diagnostic output.

sections.heading: Capstone: diagnose the failing boundary
sections.body:
A fictional service incident has these observations at one timestamp: DNS returns the expected address; a connection is established; TLS verifies the intended identity; the service returns HTTP 401 to the request. A separate state-changing request times out after being sent.

**Your task:** Identify the strongest next check for the 401 response. State what the successful observations establish and what they leave untested. Propose a bounded retry strategy for the timed-out action without exposing credentials.

**Worked solution:** The 401 response points first to missing or unacceptable authentication context at the application. Verify the intended account, credential presence and supported authentication flow without printing secret values. The observation does not prove every network condition is healthy, but it supplies no basis to blame DNS for this request. For the timeout, query the action’s status or retry using the application’s supported idempotency mechanism; do not assume it never committed.

**Check your work:** Preserve endpoint, safe request identifier, timestamps, response and each inference. Separate observed failures from untested hypotheses. Define a maximum retry count and escalation condition. A useful diagnosis narrows the failing boundary while keeping uncertainty about unobserved transaction state explicit.
sections.visual: The incident evidence narrows the first request’s failure to authentication context. It does not settle the separate timed-out action’s commit state.

do not expose credentials in diagnostics.</text></svg>

questions.q: What is the best first boundary to inspect for this 401 response?
questions.hint: Use the application response already received.
questions.answer: Authentication context: the service responded but did not accept the supplied or missing credentials for this request.

questions.q: Why is the timed-out action a separate uncertainty?
questions.hint: No response is not the same as a known rejection.
questions.answer: It may have committed before the response was lost. Status checks or supported idempotent retries are needed to avoid duplicates.

questions.q: Which observation most directly concerns the local radio link?
choices: A remote application’s response meaning
Wi-Fi signal strength
A server’s authorization decision
A database commit record
questions.explain: Signal strength measures a local radio condition rather than end-to-end service success.

questions.q: What is IP forwarding primarily concerned with?
choices: The colour of a web button
Whether a user is allowed to edit a record
Addressed packets and next hops
The meaning of a purchase request
questions.explain: IP routing and forwarding move packets without establishing application permission.

questions.q: A server returns a clear application error. What is justified?
choices: The entire internet is unavailable
Every network layer has been certified in every condition
The operation necessarily committed
Some request-response path worked, though the requested operation failed
questions.explain: A received error is useful application evidence and differs from no response, but does not prove universal health.

questions.q: What does a successful address lookup establish directly?
choices: The server committed every pending action
The remote database is healthy
A DNS record was returned for the query
The application accepted the user’s credentials
questions.explain: DNS naming evidence is separate from application availability and authorization.

questions.q: Why do caches not all change instantly after a record update?
choices: DNS has no notion of time
All records must always be permanent
Wi-Fi signal blocks record updates
Existing entries can remain reusable within their lifetimes
questions.explain: TTL-based reuse means an authoritative update and worldwide cache replacement are not simultaneous.

questions.q: What should a useful lookup incident record include?
choices: Name, returned record, resolver and timestamp
Only a screenshot colour
Only a password
Only the number of browser tabs
questions.explain: These details identify what was queried, where the answer came from and when it was observed.

questions.q: What service does TCP provide?
choices: Automatic exactly-once database commits
Preserved business-message boundaries by itself
Guaranteed zero delay
A reliable ordered byte stream
questions.explain: TCP orders and retransmits bytes; application transaction semantics remain separate.

questions.q: Which outcome is possible after an application timeout?
choices: The action committed but its response was lost
The action certainly never arrived
The action certainly completed twice
The server certainly shut down
questions.explain: A timeout leaves several possible outcomes; it is not a definitive transaction receipt.

questions.q: What helps make state-changing retries safe?
choices: Assuming UDP or TCP proves business success
Application idempotency identifiers and status checks
Retrying unlimited times with new identifiers
Only increasing screen brightness
questions.explain: Application-level deduplication and outcome queries address uncertainty across retries.

questions.q: How long to serialize 12,000 bits at 100 Mbit/s, ignoring overhead?
choices: 1.2 ms
12 ms
120 ms

questions.q: Which delay does more link bandwidth not directly remove?
choices: The time required to transmit its bits at that link
Signal propagation over a fixed path
Serialization of a fixed packet
Transfer time for a fixed payload when link-limited
questions.explain: Propagation depends on path and medium, rather than serialization rate alone.

questions.q: What is throughput?
choices: Only one-way travel time
The number of characters in a domain name
The useful data rate actually achieved
A promise that every application uses full nominal capacity
questions.explain: Throughput describes achieved delivery under the complete path and workload.

questions.q: What question does authorization answer?
choices: What the radio signal strength is
What this identity is allowed to do
How many bytes form a packet
How long DNS cached a record
questions.explain: Authorization determines permitted actions, distinct from establishing identity or connectivity.

questions.q: What does verified TLS not guarantee?
choices: A check of the intended server identity in the stated case
Integrity protection of its records
An honest uncompromised endpoint or permission for every action
Protection of the negotiated channel under its assumptions
questions.explain: Channel security has a defined boundary; endpoint behaviour and application permission remain separate.

questions.q: What is an appropriate first response to a certificate identity mismatch?
choices: Disable identity checks permanently
Publish the private key in a log
Assume the application granted access
Investigate the intended name, endpoint and trust configuration
questions.explain: The identity failure needs investigation; removing verification discards the evidence and protection.

questions.q: Which next check best follows from the observed HTTP 401?
choices: Disable TLS verification
Retry with unlimited new action identifiers
Verify intended account and accepted authentication context without logging secrets
Assume DNS failed despite its recorded answer
questions.explain: The received 401 is application authentication evidence; follow that boundary first.

questions.q: What is safest for the state-changing timeout under the stated design?
choices: Assume failure and create unlimited new requests
Declare success from TCP alone
Delete all request identifiers
Use a supported status query or the same idempotency identifier within bounded retries

questions.q: Which final claim is properly bounded?
choices: The recorded request reached the verified TLS channel and received an authentication rejection
All future service requests are guaranteed healthy
The timed-out operation certainly never committed
Wi-Fi strength proved authorization
questions.explain: The claim follows the observed request while leaving other conditions and uncertain outcomes unclaimed.

sections.title: Separate a local connection from a working service
sections.notes: They concern the local radio link, while naming, routing, transport, server state and authorization are separate dependencies. No. An application action can span multiple messages and packets, and a packet does not by itself prove the action committed.
sections.visual: The four panels describe functions with distinct evidence. The simplified layout does not imply every application uses the same transport.

sections.title: Names and addresses are different evidence
bullets: Limit: returned address is not service health
sections.notes: Resolvers and clients can reuse cached records until their cache lifetime expires under the applicable rules. Virtual hosting and certificate verification can depend on the intended name, so an IP-only request may test a different path.
sections.visual: The resolver may answer from cache rather than contacting authority every time. A returned record remains a naming result, not an application acceptance result.

sections.title: Delivery guarantees stop at a boundary
bullets: Application: defines messages and commit meaning
Retry: uncertain outcomes need idempotency or status
sections.notes: No. The application must validate, commit and report its own outcome; transport delivery alone does not establish that state. Without an idempotency key or status mechanism, a new request can create another action even when the original succeeded.
sections.visual: Transport delivery and application commit evidence are deliberately separate. A completed network exchange is not a universal transaction guarantee.

sections.title: Bandwidth is not the same as latency
bullets: Serialization: packet bits divided by link rate
sections.notes: 1,500 × 8 / 10,000,000 s = 1.2 ms, excluding additional overhead and other delays. Propagation, queuing, protocol round trips, name lookup and server processing can dominate the user-visible delay.
sections.visual: The small serialization component and larger fictional propagation component share a time unit. A faster bit rate affects only some parts of total delay.

sections.title: A secure channel does not authorize every action
bullets: TLS: channel confidentiality, integrity and identity checks
sections.notes: Yes. The channel can work while the application rejects missing authentication or insufficient authorization. A request identifier can correlate evidence across components while keeping passwords or tokens out of diagnostic output.
sections.visual: TLS protects a defined communication channel. The application still has to validate identity context and permissions for the requested action.

sections.title: Capstone: diagnose the failing boundary
bullets: Timeout: committed outcome may be uncertain
Memo: evidence, bounded retry and safe identifiers
sections.notes: Authentication context: the service responded but did not accept the supplied or missing credentials for this request. It may have committed before the response was lost. Status checks or supported idempotent retries are needed to avoid duplicates.
sections.visual: The incident evidence narrows the first request’s failure to authentication context. It does not settle the separate timed-out action’s commit state.
